title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Compliance Evidence and Exceptions
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s standards and operational procedures for: role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication; audit logging; data residency and retention; secure software development lifecycle (Secure SDLC); incident-response security procedures; compliance evidence collection and workflows; and risk & exception handling. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders responsible for architecture, operations, and evidence preparation for audits.

Scope

Applies to: all Redwood-managed services, the control plane, Redwood Console, Dedicated customer control planes, and Private deployments where Redwood provides operational guidance. For customer-managed on-prem components, follow the customer reference architecture plus this doc where applicable.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Goal: Enforce least privilege across control plane and internal tooling while supporting auditability and role separation.

Key Concepts and Roles:
- RBAC model: role -> permission set -> resource scope (organization / project / environment).
- Primary roles: Security Admin, Platform Engineer, SRE, Product Owner, Developer, Support Agent, Auditor.
- Privileged access (root/owner) is limited to 2 individuals per tenant and requires ticketed justification and 2FA + hardware key.

Role definitions (summary):
- Security Admin: manage IAM roles, approve exceptions, review change logs.
- Platform Engineer: deploy infra, manage autoscaling/config; no customer data access by default.
- SRE: incident response, runbooks, access to runtime telemetry (scoped).
- Developer: commit/build access, sandbox environments only unless elevated.
- Support Agent: customer-facing support tasks with just-in-time (JIT) ephemeral access.
- Auditor: read-only access to logs, configurations, and evidence stores.

Authentication & MFA:
- All interactive accounts require SSO via corporate IdP (Okta) with SCIM provisioned groups.
- Enforce MFA (TOTP + hardware security key for privileged roles).
- Service-to-service auth uses short-lived mTLS certificates or OIDC tokens (recommended).

Authorization Patterns and Policies:
- Use attribute-based scoping: resource tags (env:prod/dev, team:xxx) applied consistently.
- Default deny policy: new services grant no permissions until explicitly assigned.
- Approvals: role assignment for privileged roles requires manager + security approval; recorded in access-requests ticket.

Example policy (YAML pseudo):
---
role: "support-agent"
permissions:
  - "logs:view"
  - "incidents:create"
scopes:
  - "org:acme-corp:project:inference-service"
expiry: "24h"   # for JIT tokens
---

Just-in-time (JIT) Access Workflows:
1. Support Agent opens access request via internal portal, specifying scope and justification.
2. Manager approves; Security performs risk check (automated) and approves.
3. Short-lived credentials (max 24h) issued; session recorded.

2) Audit Logging

Objectives: ensure immutable, queryable, and retained audit trails for authentication events, RBAC changes, admin actions, data access, and deployment operations.

Minimum event types to log:
- Authentication: login success/failure, MFA challenge events, token issuance/refresh.
- Authorization: role assignments, policy changes, scope modifications.
- Admin actions: config changes, key rotations, DNS/TLS updates.
- Data access: object reads/writes to customer data stores, export actions.
- Infrastructure: deploys, scaling events, kernel panics, host reboots.
- Incident actions: escalation, mitigation, and forensics steps performed.

Technical requirements:
- Logs MUST be forwarded to the central logging system (Splunk/ELK/Seq) over TLS and written to an append-only store with immutability flags where supported.
- Events MUST include: timestamp (RFC3339), actor (user/service), actor_id, actor_ip, event_type, resource_id, resource_type, result, request_id, correlation_id, and human-readable reason.
- Logging service must support index-level retention policies and fine-grained access controls for auditors.

SLOs and thresholds:
- Audit ingestion: 99.9% of events indexed within 60s of emission.
- Query availability: 99.95% for last 90 days' indices.

Retention policy (default):
- Authentication and authorization events: 7 years (for enterprise/compliance customers) but searchable hot indices for 90 days, cold storage for remainder.
- Operational infrastructure logs: 1 year (hot 90 days).
- Application-level debug traces: 30 days.

Example log schema (single-line JSON string example included in docs):
{
  "ts": "2026-01-15T18:23:10Z",
  "actor": "alice@redwood.com",
  "actor_id": "u-12345",
  "event": "role.assign",
  "resource": "org:acme:project:infer",
  "result": "success",
  "request_id": "req-abc-000"
}

Tamper evidence and hashing:
- Critical audit streams (authn/authz, admin, data-export) are hashed (SHA-256) and the digest stored in the evidence store with versioned timestamps to support integrity verification.

3) Data Residency and Retention

Principles:
- Customers may choose region(s) for data residency. Control plane metadata may be global; customer data must follow selected residency constraints.
- Minimize retention of PII and secrets. Default to anonymize aggregated telemetry.

Residency controls:
- Data classification (P0-P3): P0 = customer secrets/keys, P1 = customer data with PII, P2 = telemetry/metrics, P3 = public artifacts.
- P0/P1 data stored only in customer-chosen region(s).
- Cross-region replication allowed only with explicit customer opt-in documented in contract.

Retention schedules (examples):
- P0 (keys/secrets): rotation policy and no long-term retention; backups kept for 30 days.
- P1 (customer content): default retention 7 years for enterprise contracts, 90 days for standard; configurable per-customer.
- P2 (logs/metrics): 1 year (cold store) default; 90 days hot.
- P3 (public artifacts): indefinite unless explicitly deleted.

Data deletion and verification:
1. Data deletion requests originate from API, Console, or DSAR process.
2. Deletion tasks are queued, executed per region, and a deletion report (signed) is generated.
3. Report contains resource ids, deletion timestamps, operator id, and verification digest.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle)

Goal: embed security controls across the SDLC to prevent regressions and produce evidence for audits.

Stages and controls:
- Design: threat modeling required for services that handle P1/P0 data. Owners must produce a threat model doc and mitigation backlog.
- Build: static analysis (SAST) on all PRs; dependency scanning (Snyk/OSS scanners) on merge.
- Test: unit + integration + security tests in CI; fuzzing for critical parsers; secret scanning.
- Review: at least one security reviewer for changes affecting auth, data paths, or infra.
- Release: sign-off checklist (automated gate) that enforces infra-as-code plan reviews, k8s manifests linting and rollout strategies (canary/parallel).
- Post-release: automated canary monitoring, health checks, and quality gates.

CI/CD evidence and artifacts to collect per release:
- Signed build artifact IDs, SCA report, SAST report snapshot, dependency SBOM, test coverage summary, deployment plan, and runbook link.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Objective: rapid detection, containment, and evidence-preserving remediation while maintaining clear communications.

Incident classification:
- Sev1 Security Incident: confirmed data exfiltration, keys compromise, or production tenant breach.
- Sev2: suspected unauthorized access, privilege escalation, or significant vulnerability discovered.
- Sev3: low-risk suspicious activity requiring review.

Playbook overview (high level):
1. Detection and Triage (SRE/Security)
  - Triage lead assigned within 15 minutes of alert.
  - Create incident record in incident system (Jira/PagerDuty link).
2. Containment
  - Apply temporary ACLs or network isolation; revoke affected tokens; rotate keys if indicated.
  - If production tenant affected, coordinate customer notification per legal/compliance templates.
3. Forensics (evidence preservation)
  - Snapshot relevant hosts and ephemeral storage (write-blocked where possible).
  - Preserve audit logs and compute digests; replicate to evidence bucket with immutability flag.
4. Remediation & Recovery
  - Plan and validate remediation in staging, then staged rollout.
  - Monitor canary telemetry for 48-72 hours.
5. Post-incident Review
  - Produce IR report within 7 days with timeline, root cause, scope, evidence artifacts, and action items.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Incident Commander (IC): overall coordination.
- Forensic Lead: evidence capture and chain-of-custody.
- Communications Lead: external/internal comms, legal notifications.
- Technical Leads: triage and remediation.

Evidence handling during IR:
- Maintain immutable copies of logs and disk snapshots.
- Generate signed manifests listing preserved artifacts and hashes.
- Chain-of-custody recorded in evidence system with operator identities.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose: provide consistent, auditable artifacts for SOC/ISO/PCI/enterprise audits.

Evidence types and storage:
- Policy documents (this doc and others): versioned in Confluence with access logs.
- Technical artifacts: SBOMs, SAST/SCA reports, build signatures in artifact repository.
- Operational evidence: runbooks, incident reports, capacity planning logs, backup snapshots.
- Audit logs: exported queries, hashed digests, and retention manifests.

Storage and access:
- Evidence stored in the centralized evidence bucket (s3://redwood-evidence/<year>/) with enforced encryption (SSE-KMS) and object immutability (governance mode where supported).
- Access to evidence: read-only for auditors; write access restricted to security/evidence-owners.

Workflow to produce an audit package:
1. Audit request created with scope and date range.
2. Evidence owner runs automated extractor (internal tool) to collect relevant artifacts into a time-stamped package.
3. Package validated (hashes, required artifacts checklist) and uploaded to auditor workspace.
4. Access granted via temporary signed URLs or audit-specific IAM role with expiry.

Audit timeline expectations:
- Standard SOC2 readiness package delivered within 10 business days.
- Ad-hoc evidence queries responded to within 3 business days for itemized requests.

7) Risk and Exceptions

Principles:
- Exceptions are time-limited, documented, and approved by Security and the owning Product/Engineering manager.
- High-risk exceptions (exposure of P0/P1 data, bypassing MFA) require Exec-level approval and quarterly re-review.

Exception request process:
1. Submit exception request form (internal portal) including: owner, rationale, compensating controls, duration (max 90 days), rollback plan.
2. Security performs risk assessment and either Approve / Approve with Conditions / Deny.
3. Approved exceptions produce an action plan with dates and automated reminders.

Compensating controls examples:
- Additional network segmentation, increased monitoring (higher log retention or SIEM alerts), continuous SSO revalidation, host-level EDR policies.

Exception tracking and renewal:
- All exceptions recorded in the exception register (Confluence table + ticket).
- Reminders issued 14 days before expiry; renewals require re-approval with updated risk notes.

Appendices

A. Useful commands and checks
- Verify log forwarding: curl -k https://logging-agent.local/health
- List active privileged sessions: rbac-cli sessions --filter privileged --output json
- Generate evidence package: evidence-tool collect --scope org:acme --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-01-31
